title: Loving animals
hookLine: Francis preaches to the birds (Little Flowers 16); Buddhists and Jains stress not harming

cards: A man in a rough patched habit is walking along a road in Italy with his companions when he notices trees full of birds and a field full of more. He tells his friends to wait.
Then he walks into the field and starts preaching. To the birds. The story says they don't scatter.

They stay, and listen, and don't fly off until he gives them his blessing. It's one of the stories gathered in The Little Flowers of Saint Francis, and it could be read as a charming legend and nothing more.

teach.h: FRANCIS AND HIS SISTERS THE BIRDS.
teach.b: First, Francis and his sisters the birds. In the Little Flowers, Francis addresses them as his little sisters. Most of his sermon isn't about their faults.
He reminds them how much they've been given: feathers to wear, the air to fly in, rivers and springs to drink from, and food they never had to sow or reap.
So, he tells them, beware of ingratitude, and praise your Creator. In that story, the birds aren't scenery; they're fellow creatures with their own reasons to give thanks.

teach.h: A RIGHTEOUS MAN REGARDETH HIS BEAST.
teach.b: Second, a righteous man regardeth his beast. Proverbs puts it in one short line: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast."
How someone treats an animal in their care isn't a side issue; it's part of being righteous.

teach.h: THE JAIN CARE FOR SMALL LIVES.
teach.b: Third, the Jain care for small lives. In the Jain tradition, ahimsa, not harming, reaches all the way down to the smallest living things.

The Acaranga Sutra teaches that all beings love life and dislike pain, so none should be harmed. Some Jain monks and nuns carry a soft broom to sweep insects gently from where they're about to step or sit.
Buddhists, too, place not harming living beings at the very start of their precepts.
Fourth, gentleness, small and daily: slowing down for a dog on a leash, carrying a spider outside instead of crushing it, filling the water bowl before your own coffee.
Francis called them sisters. That one word can change how a person walks past a pigeon.

how: Some Catholic and other Christian churches hold a blessing of animals on Saint Francis's feast day; Jains practice ahimsa toward all living beings, and some Jain monks and nuns sweep their path to avoid harming insects; Buddhists take a precept to refrain from harming living beings.

clap to scatter them for fun.
games.why: Francis tells his friends to wait, walks into the field and preaches to his little sisters the birds, who stay until he blesses them.

practice: Let an animal come to mind, a pet beside you, a bird outside the window, a dog from childhood, even an ant on the counter, and see it simply as a living thing, breathing too, wanting to live, avoiding pain.
Then do what Francis did in the field and name its gifts silently: fur or feathers, air, water, a way of moving that belongs to it. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for this creature.

wordCard.voice: Loving animals. Care that reaches past our own kind, the way Francis called the birds his sisters and the Jain path refuses to harm even the smallest life. Today's word.

orig.note: ahimsa, 'not harming', a Sanskrit word central to the Jain tradition and shared with Buddhists and Hindus.
